newsitem.title: NEPAL: Nepal, India to discuss treaty revision.
newsitem.headline: Nepal, India to discuss treaty revision.

text.p: Nepal's most senior career diplomat will visit India to discuss plans to revise a 47-year-old pact governing ties between the Himalayan kingdom and its giant southern neighbour, officials said on Monday.

They said Foreign Secretary Kumar Gwayali's three-day talks beginning on Tuesday with his Indian counterpart, K. Raghunath, would focus on the 1950 Treaty of Peace and Friendship between Nepal and India, which Kathmandu wants changed.
The treaty requires both countries to treat each other's citizens as their own in matters of residence, property ownership, trade and commerce.
Nepali analysts say growing immigration from India means fewer jobs and economic opportunities for Nepalis.

The treaty also obliges either country to inform the other of "serious friction or misunderstanding" with their neighbours. Analysts say the provision is violated more often than it is honoured by either side.
Foreign Minister Kamal Thapa said the talks were preliminary discussions between the two sides, agreed upon during Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's visit to Nepal in June.
Thapa told Reuters the five-month-old communist-dominated coalition government was discussing prospective changes with other Nepali political parties.
Commerce Secretary Mohan Dev Pant told Reuters Nepal had asked India for a 25 percent reduction in a countervailing duty it imposes on Nepali imports.
India, which controls about a third of the kingdom's total foreign trade, charges a countervailing duty on imports at par with excise duties imposed on its domestic products.
Last December Nepal and India signed a trade treaty that gave duty-free access to almost all Nepali products into India to boost the kingdom's exports.
Officials said landlocked Nepal was expected to start using a new route across India to reach ports in Bangladesh from September 1.

The route, agreed upon during Gujral's visit, gives transit facilities to the mountainous country, which has had access to the sea only through the eastern Indian port of Calcutta, where Nepali businessmen have complained of delays and congestion.
Under the new agreement, goods from the kingdom will be able to move through a small land corridor across northeastern India to reach ports in Bangladesh.
The new route connects Kakarvitta in Nepal with Banglaband in Bangladesh through a 71-km (44-mile) road across India, which would save on transport costs and shipping delays.
